prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: EN · Issue tracker (language en).
Grid: 6 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "ID" · longest unbreakable word 39px · one-line width 75px
  col 2: header "Title" · longest unbreakable word 92px · one-line width 394px
  col 3: header "Severity" · longest unbreakable word 59px · one-line width 59px
  col 4: header "Assignee" · longest unbreakable word 66px · one-line width 66px
  col 5: header "Status" · longest unbreakable word 61px · one-line width 77px
  col 6: header "Updated" · longest unbreakable word 62px · one-line width 87px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 360px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 359px.
This table cannot fit without splitting words at 360px. You MAY choose a total wider than 359px (the reader then scrolls horizontally), or squeeze and accept splits — a design decision.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""},"F":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

log.raw: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"good","why":"IDs and short fields stay intact and titles break at spaces, but Title is narrower than the over-wide Severity column, making many rows 4–6 lines tall; Assignee is cut at the right edge."},"B":{"grade":"good","why":"Best balance: compact ID, adequate Title, compact Severity, and no mid-word splits; only a thin sliver of Assignee shows at the right, so scrolling is required, but the visible reading order is clean."},"C":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"Titles and IDs are readable, but ID and Severity are both much wider than their short contents need, pushing Assignee, Status and Updated entirely off-screen; wasteful use of the 360px."},"D":{"grade":"bad","why":"All six columns are squeezed into tiny widths; IDs, titles, statuses and dates split mid-token (BUG-/204, progr/ess, 2024/-06-/02), making the table unreadable and untrustworthy."},"E":{"grade":"good","why":"Title gets the most room and Severity stays compact, so rows wrap reasonably; however the ID column is needlessly wide and Assignee/Status/Updated are off-screen, making it less efficient than B."},"F":{"grade":"poor","why":"The ID splits across lines (BUG-/2041), Title is too narrow and turns rows into tall stacks, while Status is only a clipped sliver; width is spent on Assignee at the cost of the identifier and main text."}},"best":["B"],"confidence":"medium","unsure":"Exact column widths are hard to measure from the screenshots, and I cannot verify whether the clipped right edge is intended as a horizontal-scroll affordance."}
